reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight emerges from repeated trial-and-error tasks where subjects perform ~3000 trials without improvement. The data shows that the most frequent response does not grow at the expense of less frequent ones, contradicting Thorndike’s law of exercise. This implies that learning cannot be modeled as a function of differential repetition frequency. Instead, the system exhibits a fixed-point attractor in response distribution. Mathematically, this suggests a Markovian process where transition probabilities between responses remain static. The failure of the law of exercise indicates that learning is not driven by reinforcement of dominant behaviors but rather by an underlying equilibrium in behavioral distribution. The implications for GSI are that Bayesian updating based on frequency will not yield improved predictions; for GSE, it means that policy transitions are not driven by reinforcement but by external stimuli alone.
